lines.text: In Ohio, an electricity bill lands in someone's mailbox.|And over the past two years or so, that bill has been creeping up.
This one piece of paper, by a long and winding route,|ends up moving *stock prices in Tokyo*.
On November 6, the Nikkei average fell *3,643 yen* in a single day.|That's the third-largest point drop on record.
lines.say: On November sixth, the Nikkei average fell three thousand six hundred forty-three yen in a single day. That's the third-largest point drop on record.

lines.text: A power bill and a stock index.|Those two feel miles apart, don't they?
But they're actually connected by *a single line*.
Hi, this is Halftick.
lines.say: Hi, this is Half Tick.

lines.text: We take the news that's scattered around in your head|and *connect it into one line*.
Today we go from a kitchen table in Ohio|to Kabutocho, Tokyo's financial district.|We'll connect the bill and the stock price on a map.
lines.say: Today we go from a kitchen table in Ohio, to Kah-boo-toe-cho, Tokyo's financial district. We'll connect the bill and the stock price on a map.

lines.text: We'll make three stops.|First, the American kitchen table. Second, the polling place.|Third, the stock market.
At the end, I'll connect all three into one line|and give you my own read.
First stop: the American kitchen table.
Right now, across the United States,|people are pushing back against new data centers.
Here's a quick guess for you.|What's a worry that keeps coming up among the people who object?
That AI will take their jobs.|That's what most of us would say, right?
One that keeps coming up is *the power bill*.
In a Reuters/Ipsos poll taken in June,|*nearly eight in ten* people said they worry|that AI will make electricity more expensive.
lines.say: In a Reuters Ipsos poll taken in June, nearly eight in ten people said they worry that A.I. will make electricity more expensive.

lines.text: And that held true no matter which party they support.
Prices really are going up.|According to government data reported by Reuters,|home electricity prices have risen *more than 10 percent* since 2024.
lines.say: Prices really are going up. According to government data reported by Reuters, home electricity prices have risen more than ten percent since twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: So why would a data center affect what a household pays?|Think of it like a neighborhood association.
Say a huge mansion moves into the neighborhood.|To serve it, the road gets widened and more streetlights go up.
The mansion pays its own electricity bill, of course.|But the cost of the road and the streetlights|gets added to the neighborhood dues.|In other words, *everyone pays*.
Power lines and power plants work in roughly the same way.
To be fair, though:|electricity isn't the only reason people object,|and data centers aren't behind the whole price increase either.
A Dallas Fed working paper estimates|that data centers have pushed up wholesale power prices|by about 2 to 6 percent.
Even so, when people look at their bill,|their eyes go to the big building going up nearby.
That's stop one.|The bill and the data center are now *connected by a line*.
Second stop: the polling place.
November 3 was the U.S. midterm election.
On that same day, in 12 states,|people also voted on local measures about data center construction.
lines.say: On that same day, in twelve states, people also voted on local measures about data center construction.

lines.text: According to a tally reported by the AP,|in *44* of the 45 measures that had been counted,|the side restricting construction won.
lines.say: According to a tally reported by the A.P., in forty-four of the forty-five measures that had been counted, the side restricting construction won.

lines.text: That's almost all of them.|And of the 47 measures in total, 21 were in Ohio.
lines.say: That's almost all of them. And of the forty-seven measures in total, twenty-one were in Ohio.

lines.text: Let's hear from someone in the opposition movement.|This is Stephen Sanders, from Texas.|Here's what he told the AP.
lines.say: Let's hear from someone in the opposition movement. This is Stephen Sanders, from Texas. Here's what he told the A.P.

lines.text: I would say data centers were on the ballot.
By the way, he's a Republican.|So you can see this isn't really a party-line issue.
In the congressional elections that same day,|Democrats won both the House and the Senate.
But let me connect these two with a *dotted line*.
We can't honestly say|that anger over power bills is what won it for the Democrats.
In the AP's voter survey,|only about one in four voters|called data centers crucial to their vote.
lines.say: In the A.P.'s voter survey, only about one in four voters called data centers crucial to their vote.

lines.text: They happened on the same day.|That's as far as the facts go.
Also, a lot of headlines said "AI regulation,"|but not a single federal law has changed.|What got decided were local rules.
lines.say: Also, a lot of headlines said A.I. regulation, but not a single federal law has changed. What got decided were local rules.

lines.text: Let's hear from the other side, too.|This is Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition, an industry group.
lines.say: Let's hear from the other side, too. This is Dan Dee-oh-ree-oh, of the Data Center Coalition, an industry group.

lines.text: We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises,|but there are going to be real-world consequences of that.
Even so, the market connected these two with a line|and reacted hard.
Third stop: the stock market.
In New York, two days after the election,|an index of semiconductor stocks|fell about *12 percent* in a single day.
According to Gaitame.com,|that was its biggest drop since March 2020.
lines.say: According to Guy-tah-may dot com, that was its biggest drop since March twenty twenty.

lines.text: The logic: if data centers don't get built,|the chips that go inside them don't get sold.|That's how investors read it.
The next day, the line crosses the Pacific and reaches Tokyo.|The Nikkei average fell 3,643 yen.
lines.say: The next day, the line crosses the Pacific and reaches Tokyo. The Nikkei average fell three thousand six hundred forty-three yen.

lines.text: Here's one more guess for you.
From Monday through Thursday of that week,|the Nikkei average fell *3.5 percent*.
lines.say: From Monday through Thursday of that week, the Nikkei average fell three point five percent.

lines.text: So how much do you think the TOPIX fell,|the index that tracks the whole Tokyo market?
lines.say: So how much do you think the Toe-picks fell, the index that tracks the whole Tokyo market?

lines.text: *0.6 percent*.|Same Tokyo stocks, and yet the gap is nearly sixfold.
lines.say: Zero point six percent. Same Tokyo stocks, and yet the gap is nearly sixfold.

lines.text: Here's why.|In the Nikkei average, companies with a higher share price carry more weight,|and AI and chip companies make up a very large part of it.
So it was *the yardstick*|most sensitive to AI news from America.
To be clear, on Friday even banks and food companies were sold,|and there was also talk that U.S. interest rates were about to rise.
So power bills alone don't explain everything.
From here, this is my own read.
What got shaken this time, I think,|wasn't faith in how capable AI is.
What got shaken was *where AI gets put*,|and *who pays its power bill*.|A much more down-to-earth problem.
Let's look at one professional view as well.|This is from a note that Dominique Toublan of Barclays|put out the day after the election.
lines.say: Let's look at one professional view as well. This is from a note that Dominique Too-blahn, of Barclays, put out the day after the election.

lines.text: AI pushback is bipartisan but local,|making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it.
Over the next four trading days,|the Nikkei average recovered about 3,400 yen.|Some say the selling was overdone.
lines.say: Over the next four trading days, the Nikkei average recovered about three thousand four hundred yen. Some say the selling was overdone.

lines.text: But the bill comes every month, doesn't it?|That doesn't stop when the election is over.
So I think this line will keep|connecting to other news from here on.
Finally, let's connect today's dots into one line.
The bill that arrived at a kitchen table in Ohio.|The "not so fast" at the polling place.
lines.say: The bill that arrived at a kitchen table in Ohio. The not so fast, at the polling place.

lines.text: Chip stocks in New York.|And the Nikkei average in Tokyo.
Connect them all, and you get:|"*America's power bills moved Japan's stocks.*"
One last thing.|In Japan, too, friction with residents|over data center construction has been reported.
If one were going to be built near your home,|would you be for it? Or against it?
If you like, tell us in the comments on Halftick.|You'll find the rest of this story at the link in the description.
lines.say: If you like, tell us in the comments on Half Tick. You'll find the rest of this story at the link in the description.
